newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Poll rumours spook French markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Poll rumours spook French markets.

text.p: French stocks plunged on Wednesday on rumours of private opinion polls which traders said showed the left well placed for the second round of the parliamentary election on Sunday.
The franc slipped to below a key level of 3.38 per mark and the Bank of France said it had no comment on market talk it was defending the currency.
Interest rate futures closed lower and bond futures closed above their lows due to late buying by domestic institutions.

"Up to now the bond market has been much more relaxed about the elections but this afternoon it has been starting to factor in a Socialist victory," Smith barney economist Stephen Englander told Reuters Financial Television.
"I think we have still some way to go," he added.
The CAC-40 share index closed down 3.63 percent or 97.17 points lower at 2,583.17, above the day's low of 2,561.23.
The drop was less pronounced than the 3.9 percent fall on Monday, which was the biggest one-day fall in four years, and followed a 0.96 percent gain on Tuesday.
Monday's fall was the biggest drop in four years.

"We are seeing a follow through from Monday. There has been a lot of complacency in the market and people did did not take fully into account that the right could lose," said Merrill Lynch strategist David Bowers.
Analysts said the stock market feared a Socialist-led government would make it harder for private companies to lay off staff and would slow down France's privatisation programme.
"Indications that the left could win the election are the catalyst for the share fall," said Gary Dugan, market strategist at J.P. Morgan.
"There are significant market concerns over the prospect of the Socialists winning the election," said Mike Young, director of European investment strategy at Goldman Sachs in London.
Economist Stuart Thomson at Banque Indosuez was more sanguine. "This is a knee-jerk panic response. We should see a recovery next week."
Analysts said the CAC-40 index could fall to 2,450-2,500 points if the left won on Sunday.
In the bond market, though, the spread between French 10-year government bonds and equivalent German bunds, a key barometer of market confidence in France, was little changed.
French bonds (OATs) were yielding nine basis points less than German bunds, compared with 10 on Tuesday.
Market analysts have said they believe a Socialist-led government would not affect France's commitment to launching a single European currency in 1999.
"What's the real difference between the left and the right? It's six of one, half a dozen of the other," a head of a French brokerage said.

Caroline Newhouse Cohen at Louis Dreyfus in Paris said that National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, tipped as a possible prime minister if the centre wins, had similar views on the need for Europe to focus on jobs and growth as Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin.

One market operator also noted that the better the Socialists' showing was on Sunday, the less dependent they would be on support from the Communist party, which has said it wants a new referendum on monetary union.
The Socialist party would need 289 seats to have an absolute majority in parliament.
A televised speech by President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday night, in which he warned French people of the danger of returning to Socialism, failed to impress the market.
French law forbids the publication of opinion polls from one week before the first round of voting. Published polls before the news blackout showed the centre-right in the lead.
